gaps.concept: Gestational age is counted from the last menstrual period, approximately two weeks before fertilization; first-trimester crown–rump length is the most accurate ultrasound dating measure.
gaps.why_tested: A stem asks for gestational age or reconciles menstrual dates with an early ultrasound.

gaps.concept: On transvaginal ultrasound, a gestational sac appears around five weeks, a yolk sac around 5.5 weeks, and an embryo around six weeks.
gaps.why_tested: An early scan shows fewer structures than expected, requiring distinction between normal timing and pregnancy loss.

gaps.concept: Early pregnancy loss is diagnostic with crown–rump length ≥7 mm without cardiac activity or mean sac diameter ≥25 mm without an embryo.
gaps.why_tested: Ultrasound measurements determine whether absent cardiac activity or an empty sac establishes nonviability.

gaps.concept: A slower hCG rise or an empty uterus alone cannot definitively diagnose ectopic pregnancy; early viable pregnancies may overlap.
gaps.why_tested: A stable patient has uncertain pregnancy location and a borderline hCG trend.

gaps.concept: Tubal inflammation or scarring impairs ciliary transport of the embryo, causing ectopic implantation.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with prior salpingitis develops a tubal pregnancy; the question asks for the underlying mechanism.

gaps.concept: An extraovarian adnexal mass or tubal ring suggests ectopic pregnancy; echogenic pelvic free fluid suggests bleeding.
gaps.why_tested: A transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and an adnexal finding.

gaps.concept: A central intrauterine fluid collection can be a pseudogestational sac; a yolk sac or embryo confirms a true gestational sac.
gaps.why_tested: An apparent uterine sac creates false reassurance in a patient with suspected ectopic pregnancy.

gaps.concept: Heterotopic pregnancy is simultaneous intrauterine and ectopic pregnancy, especially after assisted reproduction.
gaps.why_tested: An intrauterine pregnancy is visible, but pain and an adnexal mass persist after IVF.

gaps.concept: Shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation and hypotension from hemorrhage are clues to ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
gaps.why_tested: A pregnant patient develops shoulder pain, syncope, or shock despite limited vaginal bleeding.

gaps.concept: Anembryonic pregnancy is an intrauterine gestational sac that develops without an embryo.
gaps.why_tested: Ultrasound shows an empty sac meeting pregnancy-loss criteria.

gaps.concept: Retained products remain visible after incomplete abortion; the uterine cavity is empty after complete abortion.
gaps.why_tested: Bleeding follows passage of tissue, and ultrasound must distinguish incomplete from complete loss.

gaps.concept: Septic abortion presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and foul discharge; treatment requires antibiotics and uterine evacuation.
gaps.why_tested: A patient becomes febrile after pregnancy loss with retained tissue.

gaps.concept: Stable early pregnancy loss can be managed expectantly, with misoprostol, or with uterine aspiration; hemorrhage or infection favors urgent aspiration.
gaps.why_tested: A stem asks for an appropriate first-line option after confirmed pregnancy loss.

gaps.concept: Trisomy 16 is the most common autosomal trisomy found in first-trimester miscarriages.
gaps.why_tested: Cytogenetic testing after an early loss asks for the characteristic chromosomal finding.

gaps.concept: Molar pregnancy risk rises at extremes of maternal age and after a prior hydatidiform mole.
gaps.why_tested: A stem asks which patient is at increased risk of gestational trophoblastic disease.

gaps.concept: Complete moles show diffusely hydropic chorionic villi with circumferential trophoblastic proliferation; partial moles have mixed villous sizes and focal proliferation.
gaps.why_tested: A pathology image or description asks the student to distinguish complete from partial mole.

gaps.concept: Very high hCG stimulates TSH receptors because hCG and TSH share an alpha subunit, causing molar-pregnancy hyperthyroidism.
gaps.why_tested: A molar-pregnancy vignette includes suppressed TSH and elevated thyroid hormones and asks for the mechanism.

gaps.concept: Complete moles have a substantially greater risk of persistent trophoblastic neoplasia than partial moles.
gaps.why_tested: A question compares prognosis after the two histologic types of mole.

gaps.concept: Invasive mole contains hydropic chorionic villi invading the myometrium; choriocarcinoma has no villi.
gaps.why_tested: Persistent hCG after molar evacuation is paired with a myometrial pathology specimen.

gaps.concept: Gestational choriocarcinoma can follow a normal delivery, miscarriage, or ectopic pregnancy and may present with persistent postpartum bleeding.
gaps.why_tested: Vaginal bleeding and elevated hCG occur months after a nonmolar pregnancy.

gaps.concept: Placental-site trophoblastic tumor often has relatively low hCG despite tumor burden and is less chemotherapy-sensitive than other gestational trophoblastic neoplasms.
gaps.why_tested: Delayed bleeding after pregnancy accompanies a uterine mass with modest hCG elevation.
